name: Comparable Company Analysis
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Comparing Quantum Stocks to What, Exactly
lesson.summary: Comparable company analysis prices a business by referencing similar public companies' multiples, but the technique breaks down when the entire peer group is itself speculatively priced.
lesson.body:
Comparable company analysis, or comps, is a workhorse valuation method on Wall Street because it avoids forecasting an entire future cash flow stream, which is difficult to do reliably for any young company. An analyst finds public companies similar in industry, size, growth rate, and risk, calculates their multiples such as price to sales or enterprise value to revenue, and applies the resulting average or median to the company being valued. If comparable software companies trade at 8 times revenue on average, a similar private company might reasonably be valued near 8 times its own revenue, adjusted up or down for specific strengths or weaknesses relative to the peer set.

The technique depends entirely on picking a peer group that is actually rationally priced, and that is where quantum computing creates a genuine methodological problem. The natural peer group for D-Wave, IonQ, and Rigetti is each other, plus a handful of other small public and private quantum hardware and software firms. But as established under Market Valuation vs Revenue, that entire peer group trades at extreme, sentiment driven multiples rather than multiples anchored to demonstrated cash flow. Comparing one to another tells you who is relatively expensive within the group, not whether any of them is priced sensibly in an absolute sense. This is sometimes called circular comps: the peer group is comparably overpriced, so agreement with peers offers no real reassurance at all.

Work a small example. Suppose Company A trades at 150 times trailing sales, Company B at 180 times, Company C at 220 times. The average is 150 plus 180 plus 220 divided by 3, which is 550 divided by 3, about 183 times sales. An analyst might then value a fourth similar company with 10 million dollars in revenue at roughly 183 times 10 million, or 1.83 billion dollars. Every step of that arithmetic is correct, and the conclusion is still nearly worthless as a reality check, because it anchors the new valuation to the average of three numbers that may themselves be disconnected from any plausible future cash flow.

Analysts sometimes widen the comparison set to enterprise software or early stage biotech firms, where a single approval can still be years away. That is more defensible since the peers are not all part of the same narrow bubble, but it introduces its own distortions, since those industries usually have an established sales or manufacturing base a quantum company lacks. Comps work best among a rational peer set and work poorly, even dangerously, when the entire available peer set for a young sector is priced on hope rather than earnings.

Comps describe how outside investors price these companies day to day. The next concepts turn to a related but distinct question facing the venture investors who backed them privately: how they actually get their money out.
